parameters.content:
# 03 - Slack Alerts

## What this workflow does

Turns a finished decision into a card a rep can act on in ten seconds while somebody is standing in front of them. It decides **which channel**, builds the card, threads repeat visits under the person's last alert, and records whether Slack actually accepted the message. Workflow 01 calls it as a sub-flow once the classification, the CRM record and the AI synthesis are settled, and it hands back a delivery receipt: which targets were tried, what Slack answered, and every error.

## Hypotheses this design rests on

1. **The rep reads the top three lines and nothing else.** Everything below has to survive being skimmed, so the card leads with who the person is and what is blocking the decision.
2. **"New lead" is useless.** Any claim that is not self-evident carries its source inline, because the next question is always "how do you know that?"
3. **Scanner facts need no citation; public claims always do.** A rep typed the badge data. Nobody typed what the web said.
4. **A returning visitor is not a new lead, and must not be invisible either.** A repeat scan replies in the thread of the person's last card, carrying the previous booth notes, and is also broadcast back to the channel so a thread is not where a repeat goes to die. If the new classification routes to a different channel, a reply there would hide the lead from the team that now owns it, so the repeat posts a fresh card in the new channel and leaves a one-line pointer in the old thread; the next scan threads under the new card. A banner says what changed: the tier moved, the notes are new, or, said out loud, nothing changed at all - because a silent repeat is indistinguishable from a bug.
5. **An out-of-scope visit deserves a record, not a ping.** It is logged quietly with no mention, no coaching and no buttons.
6. **A Slack outage must not lose a lead.** Delivery failures are non-fatal, which only works because every outcome is recorded and asserted by the test harness.

## The logic that is implemented

**Channel names are table-driven.** The channel and the owner DM are looked up by classification in the `notifications` block of the active policy. Change a channel in the Data Table and the next scan follows it; no workflow edit. The mention rules are the exception: they are code in this workflow, not policy.

| Decision | Channel | Mention |
|---|---|---|
| `tier_1` | `#booth-hot` | `@here` + owner DM |
| `matched` | `#booth-matched` | none |
| `needs_review` | `#booth-review` | none |
| `competitor_intel` | `#competitive-intel` | none |
| `out_of_scope` | `#booth-out-of-scope` | none, and no buttons |

That table is the first scan. On a repeat scan with a material change, `matched`, `needs_review` and `competitor_intel` each get one `@here` too; `tier_1` already has one, and `out_of_scope` never gets one.

**The card is assembled in a fixed order** so the eye learns it: header (tier + the one blocker) → Prospect information → Company information → size candidates when size is unresolved → Booth notes verbatim → Why this lead → Do at the booth → links. Each group is a divider, a bold title, then the body.

**Prospect and Company blend CRM and enrichment, and every line names its own source** - badge scan, HubSpot, their website, a public source, or AI. That is the whole point of the layout: a rep can see which facts are trustworthy without asking.

**This workflow renders a decision; it does not make one.** The tier, the score and the classification arrive already settled from 01, 04 and 05. What is decided here is the channel lookup, the `@here`, the card order, the threading and the buttons. Two slots on the card are model prose - the opening question and the listen-fors - plus the decision reasons, which are printed verbatim on the out-of-scope card.

**The real bound on the model.** It cannot name a channel or add a mention: channel names come from the policy table, the mention rules from the code above. What it can do is resolve an ambiguous job title in 05, above the policy confidence floor, and a resolved persona is a different classification - so the lookup lands on a different row and the lead does move channels, as far as `#booth-hot` when 01 had already quoted an urgency trigger from the notes. A model can change which row is read; it cannot write the row. The guard that holds that line lives in 05.

**Threading is conditional on Slack confirming the root message.** The thread anchor is written only after a successful post, so a failed alert can never orphan later replies.

**A rep can move a lead, and the move comes back through here.** When someone reclassifies a lead from the card, 06 reloads the stored decision, overrides the classification and calls this workflow again - so the channel comes from the policy row for the new tier and the buttons are the ones that tier should have, with no card assembled by hand anywhere else. One `override_banner` line under the header names who moved it and why, so a repost reads as a correction rather than a duplicate scan. A review card carries all three destinations - Tier 1, Matched, Not a fit - in one row, because the only question a review card asks is where the lead belongs.

## Where it can fail

Slack can reject a card (`invalid_blocks`) or refuse a channel the app has not joined (`not_in_channel`). Both are non-fatal by design - but both come back in the delivery receipt, which 01 writes to `oak_deliveries.slack_json`, and the harness fails the test when nothing was delivered, so a silent drop is impossible. The receipt records the channel the card actually went to, read after the out-of-scope override rather than before it, so it cannot report a null channel for a card that was in fact posted. That is the lesson this workflow encodes: soft-failing is only safe when the failure is recorded.

nodes.notes: Fail-safe audit route: out-of-scope visits get one quiet card with no coaching, mentions, or action buttons.

nodes.name: Resolve Slack Targets
nodes.notes: Looks the channel and the owner DM up by classification in the policy's `notifications` block; the `slack` block only maps a HubSpot owner id to a Slack user. Channels change in the Data Table, not here.
